questions.stem: In the three-cell model of global atmospheric circulation, the Hadley cell is driven by:
options: air sinking at the poles and rising at about 60° latitude
air rising at about 30° latitude and sinking at the equator
air sinking at about 60° latitude and then rising again at the poles
air rising near the equator and sinking at about 30° latitude
questions.explanation: Intense heating near the equator makes air rise, flow poleward aloft and sink at about 30° latitude, then return towards the equator at the surface. The cell between the pole and about 60° is the polar cell, which sinks at the pole.

questions.stem: The surface winds that blow from the subtropical high-pressure belts towards the equator are the:
options: polar easterlies
jet streams
trade winds
westerlies
questions.explanation: The trade winds are the surface return flow of the Hadley cells, blowing from about 30° towards the equatorial low. The westerlies blow poleward from the subtropical highs, and jet streams are fast winds high in the troposphere, not surface winds.

questions.stem: In the Southern Hemisphere, air flowing from the subtropical high towards the equator is deflected by the Coriolis effect. The resulting trade winds blow from the:
options: south-west
west-north-west
south-east
north-east
questions.explanation: Air moving north towards the equator is deflected to the left in the Southern Hemisphere, so it arrives from the south-east. The north-east trades are the Northern Hemisphere equivalent, where deflection is to the right.

questions.stem: The Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) is a belt of:
options: high pressure where air sinks and the trade winds begin, bringing dry weather
low pressure at about 60° latitude where polar air meets the westerlies
high pressure over the poles where cold, dense air spreads towards the equator
low pressure where the trade winds meet and air rises, bringing heavy rain
questions.explanation: The trade winds of both hemispheres converge near the equator, forcing air to rise, cool and form towering cumulonimbus cloud and heavy rain. Sinking air and dry weather belong to the subtropical high-pressure belts near 30°.

questions.stem: Darwin has a wet season from about December to March and a long dry season. Which change in the global circulation best explains the wet season?
options: The belt of westerly winds moves north over northern Australia in the southern summer
The polar front moves north towards northern Australia in the southern summer
The ITCZ and monsoon trough move south over northern Australia in the southern summer
The subtropical high-pressure belt moves south over northern Australia in the southern summer
questions.explanation: The ITCZ follows the zone of greatest heating, so it shifts into the Southern Hemisphere in summer and the monsoon trough brings moist north-westerly winds and heavy rain to the Top End. In winter it moves north and the dry south-east trades return.

questions.stem: Many of the world's great hot deserts, such as the Sahara, the Kalahari and the Australian deserts, lie at about 20° to 30° latitude. In terms of the three-cell model, this is because:
options: the trade winds blow from the poles and carry very little moisture to these latitudes
the westerly winds pass over these latitudes too quickly to drop any of their moisture there
air sinking in the subtropical high warms as it descends, which suppresses cloud and rain
air rising in the subtropical low cools too slowly to condense into cloud and rain
questions.explanation: Air in the descending limb of the Hadley cell is compressed and warms, lowering its relative humidity and preventing cloud formation. The subtropics are a zone of high, not low, pressure, and the trade winds blow towards the equator from these latitudes rather than from the poles.

questions.stem: Perth and Adelaide receive most of their rain in winter, while summers are dry. Which explanation uses the global pressure belts correctly?
options: In winter the subtropical high-pressure belt shifts north, letting cold fronts in the westerlies reach southern Australia
In winter the subtropical high-pressure belt shifts further south, letting the moist trade winds reach southern Australia
In winter the ITCZ shifts south over southern Australia, bringing monsoon rain in the cooler months
In winter the polar easterlies strengthen and carry moist air from Antarctica over southern Australia
questions.explanation: The pressure belts follow the sun, so in winter the subtropical ridge lies further north and the westerlies with their cold fronts sweep across southern Australia. In summer the ridge moves south over the region, blocking the fronts and giving dry weather.

questions.stem: Which pairing of latitude zone and precipitation is predicted by the three-cell model?
options: about 60°: wetter, because air rises where polar and mid-latitude air meet
about 30°: wetter, because air rises where the Hadley and Ferrel cells meet
the poles: wetter, because cold air rises there and condenses into snow
the equator: drier, because air sinks there after crossing the oceans
questions.explanation: Precipitation is high where air rises: at the equator and along the subpolar lows near 60°, where fronts form. It is low where air sinks: near 30° and at the poles, which are cold deserts.

questions.stem: During an El Niño event in the Pacific Ocean, the usual pattern changes so that:
options: cold water upwells more strongly along the coast of Australia than usual
the Walker Circulation intensifies and rising air moves over Indonesia
the trade winds weaken and warmer water spreads east across the Pacific
the trade winds strengthen and warmer water piles up near northern Australia
questions.explanation: In El Niño the trade winds weaken or reverse, and the warm pool shifts east towards the central and eastern Pacific, taking rising air and rainfall with it. Strengthened trades and warm water near Australia describe La Niña.

questions.stem: Which combination of climate drivers would most increase the chance of drought across much of eastern and southern Australia in winter and spring?
options: La Niña in the Pacific together with a positive Indian Ocean Dipole
El Niño in the Pacific with a positive Indian Ocean Dipole
La Niña in the Pacific with a negative Indian Ocean Dipole
El Niño in the Pacific with a negative Indian Ocean Dipole
questions.explanation: El Niño moves rain-bearing rising air away from eastern Australia, and a positive IOD brings cooler water off north-west Australia, reducing moisture for rain-bearing systems crossing the continent. When both occur together the drying effects reinforce each other.

questions.stem: A winter forecast says the North Atlantic Oscillation will be in a strongly positive phase, with a deep Icelandic Low and a strong Azores High. Which outcome is most likely?
options: Strong easterlies bring dry Siberian air to the British Isles
Weak westerlies bring heavy winter rain to the Mediterranean
Strong westerlies bring mild, wet winter weather to northern Europe
Weak westerlies let very cold Arctic air settle over northern Europe
questions.explanation: A large pressure difference drives strong westerly winds and storms across the North Atlantic into northern Europe, giving mild, wet winters, while southern Europe tends to be drier. Weak westerlies and cold outbreaks are typical of the negative phase.

questions.stem: When the Arctic Oscillation is in its negative phase, the westerly winds circling the Arctic are weaker. A likely result is that:
options: the ITCZ moves north of the Arctic Circle in the Northern Hemisphere winter
warm tropical air is blocked from reaching the Arctic, so the Arctic cools
cold Arctic air moves south more easily into North America and Europe
cold Arctic air is held more tightly over the pole, giving milder winters further south
questions.explanation: Strong westerlies in the positive phase act like a fence that keeps cold air near the pole. In the negative phase the circulation weakens and buckles, allowing cold outbreaks into the mid-latitudes.

questions.stem: Why does the East Australian Current make the coastal climate of south-east Queensland and New South Wales warmer and more humid than it would otherwise be?
options: It carries warm tropical water south, warming the air and adding moisture to onshore winds
It carries cold Antarctic water north, which lowers air pressure and draws in humid air from the sea
It drives cold water upwelling at the coast, which warms the overlying air by condensation
It blocks the trade winds from reaching the coast, so warm air stays over the land
questions.explanation: Warm ocean currents transfer heat poleward and warm the air above them, and warm water evaporates readily, raising humidity and rainfall. Upwelling brings cold water to the surface and cools coastal climates, as off Peru.

questions.stem: The IPCC's Sixth Assessment Report concluded that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land. How did it describe this conclusion?
options: not yet detectable
unequivocal
likely
about as likely as not
questions.explanation: The Sixth Assessment Report stated that it is unequivocal that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land. Earlier reports used probability terms such as 'very likely' and 'extremely likely'.

questions.stem: Which piece of evidence most directly links the recent rise in atmospheric carbon dioxide to human activity rather than natural sources?
options: Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas that absorbs infrared radiation emitted by Earth's surface
The extra carbon has the isotope signature of fossil fuels and plants, not volcanoes or the ocean
Carbon dioxide levels rise and fall each year with seasonal plant growth in the Northern Hemisphere
Carbon dioxide concentrations vary between glacial and interglacial periods in ice cores
questions.explanation: Fossil fuels and plant matter are depleted in carbon-13 and fossil carbon contains no carbon-14, and both ratios in atmospheric CO2 have shifted as expected from burning them. The seasonal cycle and glacial cycles are real but natural, so they do not identify the source of the modern rise.

questions.stem: Which human land use change adds greenhouse gases to the atmosphere mainly as methane rather than carbon dioxide?
options: Converting native grassland to cropland
Expanding flooded rice paddies and cattle grazing
Clearing and burning tropical rainforest
Draining and ploughing peat wetlands
questions.explanation: Methane is produced by microbes in waterlogged, oxygen-poor soils such as rice paddies and in the digestion of ruminants such as cattle. Burning forest, draining peat and ploughing grassland release carbon mainly as carbon dioxide as stored organic matter oxidises.

questions.stem: Measurements show the lower atmosphere warming while the stratosphere above it has cooled. Why is this pattern evidence that greenhouse gases, rather than a brighter sun, are driving recent warming?
options: Stratospheric cooling is caused by the ozone layer reflecting more sunlight back to space
Greenhouse gases trap heat in the lower atmosphere, while more sunlight would warm both layers
A brighter sun would cool the lower atmosphere, while greenhouse gases warm both layers equally
Greenhouse gases are found only in the stratosphere, so they cannot warm the lower atmosphere
questions.explanation: Increased solar output would add energy throughout the atmosphere, warming the stratosphere as well. Extra greenhouse gases keep more outgoing infrared in the lower atmosphere, so less reaches the stratosphere, which cools.

questions.stem: In the Global Carbon Budget for the early 2020s, carbon dioxide emissions from land use change (mainly deforestation) were about:
options: three-quarters of total human carbon dioxide emissions
less than one-hundredth of human carbon dioxide emissions
one-tenth of total human carbon dioxide emissions
one-half of total human carbon dioxide emissions
questions.explanation: In 2023 land use change emitted about 1 billion tonnes of carbon against about 10 billion from fossil fuels and cement, so it was roughly a tenth of the total. Fossil fuels are by far the largest source, but land use change remains significant.

questions.stem: Albedo is:
options: the rate at which a surface absorbs carbon from the atmosphere
the amount of water vapour released by plants through their leaves
the proportion of outgoing infrared radiation absorbed by greenhouse gases
the proportion of incoming solar radiation that a surface reflects
questions.explanation: A surface with high albedo, such as fresh snow, reflects much of the sunlight reaching it, while a low-albedo surface, such as forest or ocean, absorbs most of it. Albedo concerns reflected sunlight, not carbon uptake or infrared absorption.

questions.stem: When tropical rainforest is cleared and burnt for pasture, how does this change natural carbon sequestration?
options: Stored carbon is released as oxygen and the land's capacity to absorb carbon is unchanged
Stored carbon is released as CO2 and the land's capacity to absorb carbon falls
Stored carbon is locked into the soil and the land's capacity to absorb carbon rises
Stored carbon is unchanged, but the pasture absorbs more carbon than the forest did
questions.explanation: Burning and decay return the carbon held in trees and soil to the atmosphere, and pasture holds far less carbon than mature forest. Deforestation is therefore a double effect: an emission now and a smaller sink in future.

questions.stem: Climate models suggest that clearing boreal forest in snowy high latitudes can have a net cooling effect, while clearing tropical rainforest has a net warming effect. What best explains the difference?
options: Boreal trees release more water vapour than tropical trees, which warms the high latitudes
Snow-covered clearings are far more reflective than dark conifers, which outweighs the carbon released
Boreal forests store no carbon, so clearing them releases no carbon dioxide to the atmosphere
Tropical clearings are more reflective than rainforest, which traps extra heat near the surface
questions.explanation: In snowy regions, dark evergreen forest masks bright snow, so clearing raises albedo strongly. In the tropics the albedo change is small and the loss of evaporative cooling and the carbon released dominate, so clearing warms the climate.

questions.stem: Mangroves, seagrass meadows and saltmarshes are described as 'blue carbon' ecosystems because they:
options: absorb carbon only from the sea water around them and never from the atmosphere
release dissolved carbon that turns coastal sea water a deep blue colour
are the main source of the carbon that forms coral skeletons on reefs
store large amounts of carbon, mostly in waterlogged soils, for their area
questions.explanation: Coastal wetlands trap organic matter in oxygen-poor sediments where it decays very slowly, so they store much carbon per hectare. Clearing or draining them releases this stored carbon.

questions.stem: A warming, drying climate increases the area burnt in a forest region, and the burnt areas regrow as shrubland. Which sequence describes a positive feedback?
options: Warming leads to more fire, more stored carbon is released, more CO2 leads to more warming
Warming leads to more fire, shrubland reflects less light, so the region cools and fires fall
Warming leads to more fire, regrowth absorbs the carbon, so atmospheric CO2 returns to normal
Warming leads to less fire, forests store more carbon, more CO2 is removed from the air
questions.explanation: A positive feedback amplifies the original change: climate change causes land cover change that releases carbon, which adds to warming. A sequence that returns the system towards its starting point is a negative feedback.

questions.stem: According to the Bureau of Meteorology and CSIRO's State of the Climate 2024, Australia's climate has warmed since national records began in 1910 by about:
questions.explanation: The 2024 report found Australia had warmed by about 1.51 °C since 1910. Most of this warming has occurred since 1950.

questions.stem: Annual temperature anomalies for a region are: 2015 +0.9 °C, 2016 +1.2 °C, 2017 +1.0 °C, 2018 +1.1 °C, 2019 +1.5 °C, 2020 +0.8 °C. A student says the 2020 value shows warming has stopped. Which response is best?
options: The 2020 value shows a cooling trend that cancels the earlier warming
The 2020 anomaly is negative, so that year was cooler than the base period
Anomalies cannot show trends because they are relative to a base period
One cooler year is natural variability; the trend must be judged over decades
questions.explanation: Climate trends are assessed over 30 years or more, because year-to-year values swing with drivers such as ENSO. The 2020 anomaly is still positive, so that year was warmer than the base period despite being cooler than 2019.

questions.stem: State of the Climate 2024 reports that cool-season rainfall has declined in south-western and south-eastern Australia in recent decades. Which future implication follows most directly?
options: More frequent snowfalls inland, so farmers must protect livestock in winter
Less runoff into dams, so cities and irrigators must find other water sources
More tropical cyclones reaching the coast, so building codes must be raised
Higher sea levels around the coast, so seawalls must be built at the ports
questions.explanation: A small fall in rainfall produces a larger proportional fall in runoff, which is why Perth has turned to desalination and groundwater replenishment. Sea level rise and cyclones are real concerns but do not follow from a rainfall decline.

questions.stem: Sea surface temperatures around Australia have risen by about 1 °C since 1900. Which current and future implication for environments follows most directly?
options: More frequent and severe marine heatwaves that cause coral bleaching
Lower rainfall over the tropics because warmer seas evaporate less water
Stronger upwelling of cold, nutrient-rich water along the Queensland coast
Faster formation of sea ice in the Southern Ocean around Australia
questions.explanation: Higher baseline sea temperatures mean that a short spell of hot, calm weather pushes water past the thresholds that corals tolerate, so marine heatwaves cause bleaching more often. Warmer seas evaporate more water, not less.

questions.stem: Coral bleaching occurs when heat-stressed corals:
options: are eaten by crown-of-thorns starfish, which leave behind white scars
expel the symbiotic algae living in their tissues, exposing the white skeleton
are smothered by a layer of pale sediment washed off nearby farmland in floods
dissolve their calcium carbonate skeletons in increasingly acidic water
questions.explanation: Corals depend on microscopic algae (zooxanthellae) that supply most of their food through photosynthesis and give them colour. Under heat stress the partnership breaks down and the algae are expelled; if the stress persists the coral may starve and die.

questions.stem: Which statement about bleached coral is correct?
options: It cannot recover, because the expelled algae never return to bleached coral
It will recover in every case, because corals always regain their algae
It is still alive and can recover if water temperatures fall soon enough
It is already dead, because bleaching happens only after the coral dies
questions.explanation: Bleached coral is stressed but alive; if heat stress eases quickly it can regain its algae. Long or severe heat stress leads to death, so outcomes depend on the intensity and duration of the heatwave.

questions.stem: The Great Barrier Reef had mass coral bleaching events in 1998 and 2002 and then in:
questions.explanation: After 1998 and 2002, mass bleaching struck in 2016, 2017, 2020, 2022 and 2024, and AIMS recorded a sixth event since 2016 in 2025. The gaps between events have shortened, leaving less time for recovery.

questions.stem: The 2022 mass bleaching of the Great Barrier Reef was significant because it was the first:
options: mass bleaching on the Reef during La Niña, normally a cooler phase there
mass bleaching ever recorded anywhere on the Great Barrier Reef or in Australia
mass bleaching to affect the northern section of the Reef
mass bleaching on the Reef in two consecutive years
questions.explanation: La Niña usually brings cloudier, cooler summers to the Reef, so bleaching in a La Niña year showed how high baseline sea temperatures have become. Mass bleaching had occurred since 1998, and 2016 to 2017 were already back-to-back events.

questions.stem: AIMS reported that the 2024 bleaching event on the Great Barrier Reef was notable because:
options: it was confined to a few inshore reefs near the mouth of the Burdekin River
it was the first time that bleaching had been recorded in the northern section
it was caused by cold water upwelling rather than by high water temperatures
it had the largest spatial footprint of any bleaching recorded on the Reef
questions.explanation: High to extreme bleaching was recorded across the northern, central and southern regions in 2024, part of a global bleaching event. Earlier events, such as 2016, were concentrated mainly in the north.

questions.stem: Degree heating weeks (DHW) add up how far sea temperatures exceed a reef's normal summer maximum, counting only weeks at least 1 °C above it, over 12 weeks. A reef is 1.5 °C above for 4 weeks, 0.5 °C above for 3 weeks, then 2 °C above for 2 weeks. What is its DHW?
options: 4 °C-weeks
6 °C-weeks
10 °C-weeks
11.5 °C-weeks
questions.explanation: Only weeks at least 1 °C above the maximum count: 1.5 × 4 = 6 plus 2 × 2 = 4, giving 10 °C-weeks. Adding the three weeks at 0.5 °C gives 11.5, but those weeks fall below the threshold and are excluded.

questions.stem: NOAA's Coral Reef Watch uses degree heating weeks to predict bleaching. Which interpretation of its thresholds is correct?
options: About 4 °C-weeks: widespread coral death is likely; about 8 °C-weeks: corals usually fully recover within a few weeks
About 1 °C-week: total reef mortality likely; about 4 °C-weeks: no bleaching expected at all
About 8 °C-weeks: bleaching begins; about 16 °C-weeks: corals first show signs of heat stress
About 4 °C-weeks: significant bleaching likely; about 8 °C-weeks: widespread bleaching and significant mortality
questions.explanation: NOAA states that significant bleaching usually occurs at about 4 °C-weeks and that by 8 °C-weeks widespread bleaching is likely and significant mortality can be expected. Higher accumulated heat stress means more severe outcomes, not recovery.

questions.stem: Scientists map the extent of a mass bleaching event across thousands of kilometres of the Great Barrier Reef. Which method is best suited to recording the pattern across hundreds of reefs in a few weeks?
options: Divers counting every bleached colony on one or two reefs over several months
A tide gauge measuring daily sea level at a port near the middle of the Reef
A survey asking tourists which reefs they thought looked most bleached
Aerial surveys scoring bleaching on each reef, checked against in-water surveys
questions.explanation: Aerial surveys cover hundreds of reefs quickly, and in-water surveys at selected sites check what the aerial scores mean. Detailed dive counts are accurate but far too slow for a reef-wide picture.

questions.stem: In the 2016 bleaching event, coral death was greatest on the northern Great Barrier Reef and much lower in the south. Mapped against sea temperature data, this pattern suggests that:
options: coral mortality increased with the amount of accumulated heat stress on each reef
corals in the south were bleached more but died less because the water was clearer
northern corals died from cyclones, which are not linked to sea temperatures
coral mortality was random and unrelated to how much heat stress each reef had
questions.explanation: Research after 2016 found that patterns of coral death closely matched the heat exposure of each reef, which was greatest in the north. About 30% of the Reef's corals died in nine months, mostly in the northern third.

questions.stem: Which is an impact of repeated coral bleaching on the ecosystem services the Great Barrier Reef provides?
options: Loss of coral lowers sea surface temperatures, so bleaching stops on nearby reefs
Bleaching increases fish numbers because bleached coral provides more food for fish
Dead, collapsing reef structure gives less habitat for fish and less protection from waves
Bleached reefs grow faster than healthy reefs, so they protect the coast from waves more effectively
questions.explanation: Living coral builds the three-dimensional structure that shelters fish and breaks waves before they reach islands and the coast. When coral dies and erodes, habitat, fisheries and coastal protection decline.

questions.stem: The Great Barrier Reef was estimated in a 2017 Deloitte Access Economics study to support about 64,000 jobs. Which group of people and places would be most directly affected by severe, repeated bleaching?
options: Office workers in Brisbane whose jobs are in state government departments
Reef tourism operators and workers in towns such as Cairns and the Whitsundays
Wheat farmers on the Darling Downs who rely on winter rainfall for their cereal crops
Coal miners in the Bowen Basin whose output depends on world coal prices
questions.explanation: Most Reef-dependent jobs are in tourism, concentrated in coastal towns that act as gateways to the Reef. A degraded reef can reduce visitor numbers and income in these places, while inland farming and mining depend on other factors.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly classifies responses to coral bleaching on the Great Barrier Reef?
options: Cutting greenhouse gas emissions is adaptation; breeding heat-tolerant corals is a mitigation
Shading reefs with brightened clouds is mitigation; cutting emissions is adaptation
Seeding reefs with coral larvae is mitigation; shading reefs with clouds is mitigation
Cutting greenhouse gas emissions is mitigation; breeding heat-tolerant corals is adaptation
questions.explanation: Mitigation reduces the cause of climate change, so cutting emissions is mitigation. Adaptation reduces harm from warming that is already happening, as with breeding heat-tolerant corals or shading reefs during marine heatwaves.

questions.stem: Researchers are trialling marine cloud brightening, which sprays fine sea-salt mist to make low clouds more reflective over parts of the Reef during heatwaves. Which is the best evaluation of this response?
options: It may cut local heat stress for a time but does not address rising global temperatures
It solves the bleaching problem permanently by lowering ocean temperatures across the whole world
It is a mitigation response because it removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere
It is ineffective because clouds have no influence on the light reaching the sea
questions.explanation: Brighter clouds reflect sunlight and could reduce light and heat on targeted reefs during a heatwave, buying time. It treats a symptom at a local scale, so cutting global emissions is still needed to address the cause.
